AAON_2017q3: AAON entered the August 2017 report off a weak first quarter — flat sales, earnings down 11.5% — but backlog jumped 40.9% to $68.9 million, shifting focus toward whether order recovery would show up in shipments. Coverage was thin, with no major catalysts beyond a routine dividend.
AAON_2018q4: AAON entered November 2018 with record demand but deteriorating profitability: Q2 sales rose 8.2% while net income fell 15.2%, even as backlog surged 87.5%. Management had already flagged the fix — pricing and better throughput — so investors were watching whether the causes looked temporary and demand stayed intact.
AAON_2019q2: AAON entered May 2019 mid-recovery: 2018 sales hit a record but margins had compressed on labor and material costs, with fixes underway. The stock had already run up sharply, so investors wanted proof price increases were finally offsetting costs and record backlog would convert into profitable, not just larger, volume.
AAON_2019q4: Heading into October 2019, the question was whether AAON could convert strong demand into shipments. The prior quarter had missed estimates, with management blaming sheet-metal equipment downtime, not weak orders. AAON ordered more fabrication machines and committed to a Texas expansion, underscoring capacity, not demand, as the constraint.
AAON_2020q1: AAON entered February 2020 still testing whether new fabrication capacity added in Q3 2019 would lift throughput and margins after a nearly flat quarter. The report landed the same day a coronavirus-driven selloff pushed the S&P 500 into correction, meaning any positive reaction had to reflect strong, company-specific news.
AAON_2020q2: The months before AAON's May 2020 report shifted the debate from execution to pandemic resilience, after a strong February quarter showed new equipment improving throughput. AAON rush-produced HVAC units for a temporary COVID hospital in New York, and saw an operations leadership transition as its longtime VP retired.
AAON_2021q4: AAON entered November 2021 with demand clearly outrunning its ability to produce profitably. Q2 sales hit a record with backlog up 33% and bookings up roughly 70%, so demand wasn't in question — margins were, on labor and material cost pressure. The stock also entered from a position of strength.
AAON_2022q3: AAON entered August 2022 with a damaged profitability story: an earlier earnings miss and market weakness had pressured shares, as inflation and low-priced backlog absorbed the benefit of strong revenue growth. Price increases and the BasX acquisition were underway, but much of the backlog still predated those price actions.
AAON_2023q1: AAON entered February 2023 with the debate shifting from whether pricing could catch inflation to how fast the company could convert its backlog at improved margins. A weak mid-2022 quarter had given way to improving efficiency. The stock hadn't run up sharply beforehand, leaving room for a genuine surprise.
AAON_2024q1: AAON entered February 2024 after an exceptionally strong 2023, with the question shifting from operational recovery to whether it could sustain high margins and growth as comparisons got harder and construction softened. Full-year sales had risen over 30% and income over 75%, so investors approached confident rather than skeptical.
AAON_2024q4: AAON entered November 2024 on strong momentum: an exceptional August quarter beat estimates, repairing a weak first-quarter stumble. The bigger catalyst came in October, when AAON disclosed roughly $174.5 million in data-center liquid-cooling orders, turning a qualitative pipeline story into a booked one. Shares were already up about 37%.
ABM_2018q1: ABM entered March 2018 after a rough December report that had missed earnings and cut guidance, sending shares down roughly 16%. Investors approached still skeptical about the cost of the GCA acquisition and its 2020 Vision transformation, watching for evidence that integration risk was stabilizing enough to revalue the deal.
ABM_2018q2: ABM entered Q2 2018 with a sharp gap between improving guidance and poor stock performance — shares had lost roughly a third of their value over the year and sat near a 52-week low, even after Q1 raised EPS guidance. The market remained skeptical about GCA costs and wage pressure.
ABM_2018q3: The months before Q3 2018 followed an unusual June combination — an earnings beat paired with lower full-year guidance. Investors had evidence demand was healthy but labor, overtime and integration costs were still eating into profit. The persistent question was portfolio realignment and GCA integration, not a single new event.
ABM_2018q4: ABM entered fiscal Q4 2018 after a year of repeated doubts about whether GCA and the 2020 Vision transformation could deliver enough margin improvement to justify their cost. Year-end results were a credibility test for the full strategic plan, with new bookings watched as forward indicators.
ABM_2019q1: ABM entered Q1 2019 right after a major re-rating — the December report had beaten estimates, declared GCA integration complete, and set strong new guidance, driving a +20% two-day rally. That raised the bar considerably: investors now needed proof the strong year-end narrative could persist.
ABM_2019q2: ABM entered Q2 2019 after a March quarter that had reportedly beaten earnings but still failed to produce a positive stock reaction. Consensus expected further EPS growth, extending a streak of four consecutive beats, but the lingering question was earnings quality — whether margin gains reflected real integration progress.
ABM_2019q3: ABM entered Q3 2019 after a strong prior beat, but analyst estimates had begun softening, revised about 1.5% lower in the month before the report. The market was balancing a good beat history against concern that labor and macro pressure could slow the ongoing transformation story.
ABM_2019q4: ABM entered Q4 2019 after a difficult autumn — Q3 had produced record revenue and a modest beat, yet shares still declined amid broad downward estimate revisions. The question was whether ABM could finish the year strongly enough to show its pricing and labor discipline was working.
ABM_2020q1: ABM entered Q1 2020 with improving momentum after Q4 rebuilt some credibility, but growing coronavirus uncertainty was starting to dominate markets. Exposure looked ambiguous — closures could cut janitorial and aviation work, while heightened cleaning needs could boost demand — though the report landed just before the full shutdown hit.
ABM_2020q2: The months before Q2 2020 were dominated by COVID-19: ABM's services were designated essential, and clients began demanding infection-control work. Traditional activity in aviation and education was collapsing while higher-margin virus-protection work offered a partial offset, making labor flexibility the central question rather than simple revenue decline.
ABM_2020q3: ABM entered Q3 2020 after a powerful June relief rally driven by evidence that higher-margin COVID work and cost flexibility could offset the pandemic's revenue hit. The question shifted from survival to durability — would enhanced cleaning demand persist as facilities stayed partly closed?
ABM_2020q4: ABM entered Q4 2020 with an already-understood pandemic-era model: pressured normal revenue offset by unusually strong margins from virus-protection work and tight labor management. Q3 had delivered EPS growth and over $130 million of operating cash flow despite a 15% revenue decline.
ABM_2021q1: ABM entered fiscal Q1 2021 after a year in which COVID cleaning demand transformed its margin profile; Q4 produced record cash flow, but the market was already questioning whether that could persist as offices reopened. The test was whether temporary demand could convert into a durable service relationship.
ABM_2021q2: ABM entered Q2 2021 after an exceptional quarter in which virus-protection work and labor discipline drove record profit, raising the bar for proof that strength could broaden beyond temporary cleaning demand. The tension was reopening reviving traditional services versus emergency disinfection work fading from the mix.
ABM_2021q3: ABM entered Q3 2021 with a stronger core business plus a major new deal — the $830 million Able Services acquisition announced in August. That reintroduced integration and leverage risk after years digesting GCA, so investors weighed reopening-driven growth against execution risk from a second large acquisition.
ABM_2021q4: ABM entered Q4 2021 with two major shifts underway: the Able Services acquisition and a new ELEVATE transformation program. The market had to price integration costs and financing risk, with consensus already expecting roughly $0.80 EPS — a beat alone wasn't enough without reassurance spending wouldn't eat the benefit.
ABM_2022q1: ABM entered Q1 2022 after a December selloff had already reset expectations around ELEVATE and Able integration costs — investors knew the transformation would be expensive. Russia's invasion of Ukraine added exceptional macro volatility, pushing energy prices sharply higher, a risk for a labor- and fuel-intensive service company.
ABM_2022q2: ABM entered Q2 2022 on a constructive setup — Q1 had produced 9.1% organic growth and raised guidance — but investors worried about growth quality, as COVID disinfection work declined and ELEVATE spending ramped. The question was whether normalized demand could replace pandemic-era profitability without hurting margins.
ABM_2022q3: ABM entered Q3 2022 after a June selloff in which the market rejected a headline earnings beat because EBITDA margin and cash flow deteriorated as pandemic cleaning work normalized. Margin quality, not revenue growth, became the central question, with the stock already punished for mix concerns.
ABM_2022q4: ABM entered fiscal Q4 2022 after two straight quarters where beats failed to produce durable stock gains, as EBITDA margin kept compressing while the business mix shifted from pandemic work toward acquired, lower-margin services. Investors needed proof pricing and cost control could stabilize profitability by year-end.
ABM_2023q1: ABM entered Q1 2023 still digesting a year of acquisition-driven revenue growth against uneven margins — Q4 had modestly beaten estimates yet shares still fell. Consensus expected roughly $0.77 EPS, with the key question being whether labor, interest expense and ELEVATE spending pressure would finally begin to ease.
ABM_2023q2: ABM entered Q2 2023 after a mixed March quarter where EPS beat but revenue missed and margins stayed pressured. Focus centered on whether pricing and cost control could offset labor and interest expense, while the RavenVolt acquisition offered a potential mix improvement if higher-value projects grew faster.
ABM_2023q3: ABM entered Q3 2023 after a June quarter that finally delivered the margin improvement investors wanted, with EBITDA margin and cash flow both rising. That raised the bar for September, even though shares remained down roughly 13% year-to-date, suggesting the market stayed cautious despite the improvement.
ABM_2023q4: ABM entered Q4 2023 after one of its worst reactions in the dataset — shares fell sharply in September following an EPS miss and a cut to the top end of guidance. December became a credibility test for whether that deterioration was temporary, with consensus around $0.92 EPS.
ABM_2024q1: ABM entered Q1 2024 after a strong December rebound in which earnings, margins, cash flow and capital return all improved. The question shifted again — could ABM sustain that recovery while still funding ELEVATE and technology investments, given the stock had already responded positively to the prior beat?
ABM_2024q2: ABM entered Q2 2024 with improving stock momentum — a rising relative-strength rating and a constructive technical pattern followed a March quarter with 9% earnings growth. Expectations were no longer depressed, so the key issue remained margin: Q1 beat estimates yet EBITDA margin declined on technology and interest costs.
ABM_2024q3: ABM entered Q3 2024 after a strong June reaction, another guidance raise and improved cash generation, setting a higher bar for September. Investors increasingly wanted proof that promised margin expansion would arrive, while the newly announced $119 million Quality Uptime Services acquisition added a fresh integration consideration.
ABM_2024q4: ABM entered fiscal Q4 2024 after a September quarter that beat on EPS and revenue but still failed to produce a durable stock gain, reinforcing the market's focus on margin and cash-flow quality over headline beats. Investors wanted proof Technical Solutions and data-center exposure could lift profitability.
ABSI_2022q3: Absci entered August 2022 from a very depressed stock base — shares had lost roughly three-quarters of their value that year. Despite an early-stage biotech's typical cash burn, the company added momentum: a seven-program antibody-drug-conjugate collaboration in July, plus ongoing Merck and NVIDIA partnerships and a new NY AI lab.
ACCO_2019q3: ACCO entered July 2019 waiting for proof that pricing and consumer diversification could offset tariffs and weak legacy office demand. Recent moves included launching the TruSens air-purifier brand alongside Kensington. The key question was whether back-to-school demand and price increases would translate into stronger operating income for the full year.
ACCO_2019q4: ACCO entered October 2019 after a very strong July reaction — record sales, better margins, higher guidance. During the window it acquired Brazil-based Foroni for about $57 million and authorized $100 million more in buybacks. With the bar raised, Q3 needed to prove margins could hold as seasonal mix normalized.
ACCO_2020q1: ACCO entered February 2020 after a sharp negative reaction to Q3, which showed weaker margins, lower adjusted EPS and unfavorable mix despite record free cash flow. EMEA sales were down 5.9% for the year, softening mid-year before stabilizing. Expectations were low, centered on whether earnings growth could re-establish itself.
ACCO_2021q1: The months before February 2021 were dominated by COVID: legacy office and school demand stayed depressed while Kensington, air purifiers and home-use products benefited from remote work. ACCO also acquired gaming-accessories maker PowerA in December 2020, adding a faster-growth consumer category but also new leverage and integration risk to weigh.
ACCO_2021q2: ACCO entered Q1 2021 with a split narrative: February had shown severe COVID damage to legacy office demand, but newly acquired PowerA offered a faster-growing consumer/gaming platform and EMEA showed relative resilience. Investors wanted proof PowerA's growth and integration justified its price, and that e-commerce categories could keep growing.
ACCO_2022q1: ACCO entered Q4 2021 after a year of strong reopening and PowerA momentum, with the earlier report showing PowerA outperforming. The market wanted to know if those gains could persist as demand normalized and cost inflation intensified. Consensus sat near $0.48 EPS, with the stock down over the prior year.
ACCO_2022q2: ACCO entered Q1 2022 with strong momentum after management forecast another record year, backed by PowerA and reopening demand plus a strong Q4 reaction. The emerging risk was no longer demand but whether inflation, logistics and raw-material costs would outrun pricing actions supporting the already-guided full-year earnings growth.
ACCO_2023q1: ACCO entered February 2023 after a harder second half of 2022 than expected, as inflation, FX and retailer destocking hurt gaming and North American profit. Full-year EPS guidance had been cut materially during the year, leaving investors with low confidence in visibility and a preference for conservative guidance.
ACCO_2023q2: ACCO entered Q1 2023 on low expectations after February showed falling sales, a small EPS miss and weak retailer/gaming demand, with 2023 guidance leaning on price realization, lower freight costs and restructuring. Investors were no longer rewarding revenue growth alone — they wanted proof those margin self-help levers were working.
ACCO_2024q1: ACCO entered Q4 2023 after a year of margin and cash-flow repair despite weak destocking-driven demand and slow office return. Shares had already risen roughly 25% over three months, and a late-January restructuring plan targeting $60 million in annual savings raised the bar for guidance to show savings outpacing pressure.
ACMR_2019q2: ACM Research entered May 2019 with strong momentum — Q4 2018 revenue up over 20%, and the company turned profitable after a 2017 loss. Management targeted roughly $100 million for full-year 2019, and January's Tahoe tool delivery to a key customer reinforced the case for expanding beyond a narrow base.
ACMR_2019q3: ACM entered August 2019 after Q1 revenue doubled year over year and returned to profitability, with a roughly $100 million full-year target intact. The company also pursued a STAR Market listing for its Shanghai unit to fund China expansion, with customer wins the key question.
ACMR_2020q1: ACM entered March 2020 after a record Q3 2019 — revenue up 44.2%, margin 48.6% — expanding capacity with a new Shanghai R&D center funded by roughly RMB 416 million in private investment. COVID-19 then shifted the question from how fast ACM could grow to how much survived a shutdown.
ACMR_2022q4: ACM entered Q3 2022 after a volatile stretch: a COVID-hit Q1, then a Q2 revenue jump of 93.8% sending shares up over 20%. That recovery was hit by new U.S.-China chip export controls, sending the stock down roughly 26.5% in October, before Shanghai disclosed strong preliminary Q3 revenue and backlog.
ACMR_2024q1: ACM entered February 2024 with shares already up roughly 29% over three months and over 100% over a year, after January guidance raised 2024 revenue targets to $650-725 million on China semiconductor investment and new international customers. Expectations were already high going in, not a depressed base.
ACVA_2021q4: ACV entered November 2021 with a disconnect between strong growth and a de-rated stock — August's Q2 report showed revenue up 117% and raised guidance, yet shares had fallen roughly 27% over three months as investors questioned whether growth would survive normalizing used-car prices and continued heavy investment despite losses.
ACVA_2023q1: ACV entered February 2023 after a weak November print (EPS miss, revenue below consensus) left shares down about 19% year-to-date and over 70% off their high. Falling wholesale used-car prices had lowered guidance, so expectations going in were low — investors wanted cost control and margin progress, not hypergrowth.
ADMA_2017q2: ADMA entered May 2017 mid-transaction — January's Biotest acquisition promised to make it a vertically integrated plasma-products company with direct control over remediating RI-002's manufacturing issues. Q1 showed the transition's cost: revenue missed estimates and losses widened, though much of the excess expense was one-time, deal-related cost.
ADMA_2017q4: ADMA entered Q3 2017 just after closing the Biotest acquisition, adding manufacturing operations, Nabi-HB and BIVIGAM plus direct control over FDA remediation. Q2 had shown roughly 50% sequential sales growth and early synergies, balanced against a larger cost base — weighing greater commercial potential against real regulatory and integration risk.
ADMA_2018q1: ADMA entered March 2018 still focused on remediating its Boca manufacturing facility — BIVIGAM remained off-market and RI-002 couldn't advance until FDA compliance was resolved. The 2017 Biotest deal had more than doubled revenue and made ADMA vertically integrated, but remediation costs, facility expenses and debt kept pushing losses higher.
ADMA_2018q2: ADMA entered May 2018 two months after heavy 2017 losses, with dilution layered atop regulatory risk since Biotest held a large equity stake from the 2017 deal. Just before the report, ADMA negotiated the return and retirement of roughly 8.6 million shares, cutting shares outstanding by about 19%.
ADMA_2018q4: ADMA entered late 2018 with regulatory progress but no full commercialization yet. An FTC review of Grifols' Biotest deal confirmed Grifols wouldn't acquire Biotest's ADMA stake, removing one ownership uncertainty. Boca's compliance had improved enough to move toward new submissions, with investors waiting for BIVIGAM's supplement and RI-002's review.
ADMA_2019q1: ADMA entered March 2019 at a more advanced stage: Boca achieved VAI classification, debt was refinanced with Perceptive Advisors, and RI-002 carried an April 2 PDUFA date alongside a pending BIVIGAM review. But 2018 revenue fell to about $17 million while the net loss widened to roughly $65.7 million.
ADMA_2019q2: The months before May 2019 were transformational: RI-002 (rebranded ASCENIV) won FDA approval, ADMA gained a fifth patent and a new Perceptive Advisors credit facility. The narrative shifted from 'will the lead product clear the FDA' to 'how fast can ADMA commercialize two immunoglobulin products,' removing a major binary risk.
ADMA_2021q2: ADMA entered Q1 2021 with ASCENIV and BIVIGAM launches finally generating recurring revenue, though scale to profitability was still needed. Pandemic disruption made plasma supply strategically critical, and in February ADMA won FDA approval for a new Knoxville, Tennessee collection facility, reducing dependence on external plasma.
ADMA_2023q2: ADMA entered Q1 2023 after a major commercial turnaround — moving from regulatory remediation into rapid ASCENIV/BIVIGAM adoption, with management already guiding to over $210 million of 2023 revenue. The main question was whether that revenue scale would finally push the company through adjusted EBITDA breakeven.
ADMA_2024q1: ADMA entered Q4 2023 after a breakthrough year — Q3 had already delivered positive EPS and a sizable revenue beat, with ASCENIV adoption increasingly treated as a durable growth driver. January's preliminary guidance came in above prior assumptions, raising the bar heading into the report.
ADMA_2024q3: ADMA entered Q2 2024 with extraordinary momentum: May's Q1 report beat on EPS and revenue and raised 2024/2025 guidance, sending shares up about 23%. Investors were already rewarding accelerating ASCENIV growth, so Q2 carried a high bar to justify the rerating with another large beat.
ADT_2018q1: ADT's first earnings report came less than two months after a difficult IPO — shares priced at $14 (below range) and opened around $12.65, reflecting skepticism about a highly leveraged model facing cheaper DIY and smart-home competitors. With the stock already below IPO price, tolerance for disappointment was unusually low.
ADT_2018q2: ADT entered Q1 2018 after a severe post-IPO de-rating and a March report that failed to reassure investors on leverage and profitability. With no major acquisitions in between, attention stayed narrowly on subscriber economics — attrition, recurring revenue, adjusted EBITDA and the cash required to add customers.
ADT_2018q3: ADT entered Q2 2018 with some customer-economics improvement but no real change in the valuation debate — Q1 showed lower attrition and higher EBITDA, yet shares fell as investors doubted gains would reach net earnings. A preferred-securities redemption trimmed one costly capital layer but not the broader debt burden.
ADT_2018q4: ADT entered Q3 2018 after a large August disappointment, but the story broadened: a September Amazon/Alexa integration offered a way to participate in smart-home competition rather than fight it, and a late-October deal to acquire Red Hawk Fire & Security expanded commercial security, shifting focus beyond residential attrition alone.
ADT_2019q1: ADT entered Q4 2018 after a much stronger November report and the completed Red Hawk acquisition, with attrition and free cash flow stabilizing and Amazon integration adding a smart-home channel. The bar was meaningfully higher than in August — a disappointment would challenge the whole recovery narrative's credibility.
ADT_2019q2: ADT entered Q1 2019 two months after a major guidance-driven selloff — March produced an adjusted loss versus expected profit and a weaker outlook, followed by a notes offering that kept leverage in focus. The market wanted rapid credibility repair: stronger earnings and proof Red Hawk could offset costs.
ADT_2019q4: ADT entered November 2019 after another rough August reaction (shares down over 12% on an adjusted loss despite a slight revenue beat). The window also included the Canadian-operations sale, debt refinancing and a planned special dividend, moves that could produce relief even with the leverage debate unresolved.
ADT_2020q1: ADT entered Q4 2019 after a strong November reaction and a year of portfolio restructuring — Canada-sale proceeds funded debt actions and shareholder returns, while commercial revenue accelerated. Coronavirus risk was emerging by March, but ADT's outlook explicitly assumed no material COVID impact just as markets began repricing the pandemic.
ADT_2020q2: The months before Q1 2020 were dominated by COVID-19 — ADT's March outlook assuming no material pandemic impact became obsolete as lockdowns spread. Investors focused less on ordinary variance and more on payment behavior and whether recurring monitoring revenue would hold up, with cash-flow quality most important.
ADT_2020q3: ADT entered Q2 2020 earnings just two days after Google agreed to invest $450 million for a 6.6% stake and partner on smart-home security — shares surged roughly 57%. The report landed after an enormous re-rating, so any negative reaction could reflect profit-taking rather than a poor quarter.
ADT_2020q4: ADT entered Q3 2020 with the August Google partnership as the dominant strategic anchor, though shares had given back part of the initial surge. Investors wanted evidence Google/Nest integration could drive faster subscriber growth rather than remain a distant promise, alongside signs of commercial recovery and debt reduction.
ADT_2021q1: ADT entered the 2020 year-end report with Google development on track and improving customer retention, plus early debt paydown using cash. The market wanted a 2021 outlook translating those gains into faster growth, making the stock sensitive to how much subscriber-acquisition and technology spending would pressure near-term cash flow.
ADT_2021q2: ADT entered Q1 2021 after an exceptionally negative February reaction to the cost of accelerating growth — investors had accepted lower near-term free cash flow for Google-driven expansion. The next report needed to show spending was improving customer metrics; a revenue beat mattered less than proof the program worked.
ADT_2021q3: ADT entered Q2 2021 after showing better subscriber growth and retention in May, setting a straightforward bar: keep the earnings burden controlled while recurring revenue kept expanding. The Google platform story remained central, but the market had grown more disciplined about near-term economics after February's selloff.
ADT_2021q4: ADT entered Q3 2021 after a severe August EPS-driven selloff that lowered expectations for the core security business. On the reporting date itself, ADT announced the roughly $825 million Sunpro Solar acquisition and launch of ADT Solar, a major new capital-intensive bet just as investors demanded better earnings discipline.
ADT_2022q1: ADT entered Q4 2021 with Sunpro Solar as the newest piece of the thesis, initially well received but raising questions about integration cost and cash-flow dilution. The core security business stayed stable, making the quarter a baseline for separating legacy monitoring economics from the newly acquired solar operation.
ADT_2022q2: ADT entered Q1 2022 after a surprisingly positive reaction to a quarter that missed EPS but beat revenue, setting a new framework: the market would tolerate near-term earnings weakness if security revenue and solar growth built a credible path to higher long-run value, so long as leverage didn't compound further.
ADT_2022q3: ADT entered Q2 2022 after two quarters of EPS misses the stock had tolerated, on the belief security revenue was stable and Sunpro/ADT Solar would eventually broaden household economics. By August, management had enough history for a clearer sense of solar's trajectory — momentum mattered more than one quarter EPS.
ADT_2022q4: The months before Q3 2022 held one of ADT's biggest announcements since Google: State Farm agreed to invest roughly $1.2 billion at $9/share plus up to $300 million for innovation, with Google adding $150 million more — shares surged about 16%. Investors asked if operations could support that valuation.
ADT_2023q1: ADT entered Q4 2022 with a stronger strategic anchor after State Farm and Google's capital commitments and a Q3 EPS beat, raising the bar for 2023 guidance. ADT Solar remained the uncertainty, more cyclical and complex than security, so year-end results needed to show it wouldn't dilute margins.
ADT_2023q2: ADT entered Q1 2023 after February had already reset expectations sharply lower, with full-year EPS guidance cut well below prior consensus amid worries that ADT Solar was undermining an otherwise stable security franchise. Since the stock was already de-rated, May needed to confirm guidance had fully captured the problem.
ADT_2023q3: ADT entered Q2 2023 after the year's largest selloff, following a May report exposing weak solar economics and a revenue/outlook problem. Investors increasingly wondered if management should simplify the portfolio rather than fund every business line, with debt reduction from an asset sale looking more valuable than growth.
ADT_2024q1: The months before February 2024 marked a major reset: ADT sold its commercial business for $1.6 billion in October, mostly for debt reduction, then announced exiting residential solar on January 25 — shares rose about 11% alongside a dividend hike and buyback, rewarding a return to the security core.
ADT_2024q2: ADT entered Q1 2024 two months after a powerful earnings re-rating and three months after the solar exit, with a cleaner thesis: security-only focus, debt reduction, capital returns. That momentum was interrupted in March when Apollo's large secondary offering pressured shares, adding technical overhang despite improving core fundamentals.
AES_2017q1: AES entered February 2017 mid-portfolio-reset — reducing parent debt, exiting weaker generation, and just before the report agreeing to acquire sPower, a major U.S. solar developer with over 10 GW in pipeline. The stock faced two narratives: legacy merchant/coal exposure and leverage versus a rapidly expanding contracted renewables platform.
AES_2017q2: The months before Q1 2017 saw AES advance its year-end strategy: completing more of the sPower solar push, restructuring the Alto Maipo hydro project, prepaying $300 million of parent debt, and continuing to exit merchant coal. Investors wanted evidence the cleaner portfolio could still deliver near-term earnings despite restructuring costs.
AES_2017q3: AES entered Q2 2017 after a constructive Q1 — sPower closed, the 1.4 GW Southland project was financed, and new capacity came online. The main blemish was Alto Maipo in Chile, where cost overruns grew visible. With 2017 guidance reaffirmed in May, August tested whether margins could absorb that risk.
AES_2017q4: The months before Q3 2017 brought two new risks: Alto Maipo execution concerns, and Hurricanes Irma and Maria damaging AES assets in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands just before quarter-end. AES was accelerating portfolio simplification, raising its asset-sale target and forming the Fluence storage venture with Siemens.
AES_2018q1: AES entered early 2018 after 2017 closed with hurricane damage, Alto Maipo risk and a raised asset-sale target, emphasizing a faster coal exit and a bigger pivot to contracted gas, renewables and storage. The question was whether debt reduction and new projects were improving earnings, not just shrinking the portfolio.
AES_2018q3: By mid-2018 AES had completed the Eletropaulo sale, brought cleaner gas generation online and kept cutting parent leverage, continuing its shift from a global generation conglomerate toward a simpler contracted-growth model. The question remained whether debt reduction and new projects were improving earnings, not just shrinking the portfolio via disposals.
AES_2018q4: AES entered the period with positive strategic momentum, continuing asset sales, carbon-intensity reduction and management succession planning as part of its shift toward a simpler contracted-growth model. Investors wanted evidence these actions were raising margins and cash flow, not just producing a temporary boost from disposals.
AES_2019q1: AES entered the 2018 year-end report after a year of aggressive simplification — asset sales, parent debt reduction, new contracted capacity and a public commitment to lower carbon intensity. Investors increasingly valued AES as a deleveraging/renewables-growth story, so the report needed to extend that narrative on leverage and backlog quality.
AES_2019q2: AES entered the period with a newly set 7%-9% long-term growth target, a 5.8 GW project backlog and continued parent-debt reduction. Investors focused less on absolute revenue and more on the pace of renewable project conversion, interest savings and how much asset-sale disposals were diluting near-term earnings.
AES_2019q3: As in the prior quarter, AES's story centered on its 7%-9% long-term growth target, 5.8 GW backlog and ongoing parent-debt reduction. Investors wanted quarterly earnings to validate the cleaner, contracted-growth model even as legacy-business exits shrank the earnings base, watching renewable conversion pace and utility performance closely.
AES_2019q4: Heading into this report, AES's setup remained the same 7%-9% growth target and 5.8 GW backlog story, with continued parent-debt reduction. The market kept weighing whether renewable project conversion and interest savings were offsetting the earnings drag from ongoing asset sales and legacy-business exits.
AES_2020q1: AES entered the 2019 year-end report with a multi-year plan built on renewables backlog conversion, debt reduction and investment-grade credit, just as COVID-19 triggered a severe selloff around the reporting date. Its utility and long-term contracted generation base offered more expected resilience than cyclical sectors, though construction risk remained.
AES_2020q3: By August 2020, the market had learned AES's contracted, utility-heavy model was relatively resilient through COVID, so focus returned to renewables contracting, coal exits and credit ratings, and whether execution stayed on schedule despite pandemic disruption — a test of whether the crisis delayed the transformation or was just noise.
AES_2020q4: AES entered Q3 2020 after a powerful August re-rating, with investors already expecting the pandemic-resilient transition to continue, raising the bar to real progress on credit ratings, coal exits and renewables contracting, not just maintained earnings, while low rates made refinancing parent debt an added focus.
AES_2021q1: AES entered the 2020 year-end report after earning a second investment-grade rating, cutting coal exposure below 30% and refinancing parent debt, a materially strengthened narrative. Investors wanted a 2021 outlook that could sustain the re-rating, with renewables contracting and storage, via Fluence's leading position, now central to the thesis.
AES_2021q3: Between February and August 2021, AES accelerated its clean-energy thesis: U.S. utilities won approvals for over $2 billion of rate-base investment, large new renewable PPAs were signed, and Moody's moved its outlook to positive. Q2 needed to show financial delivery and strategic throughput, especially technology-customer demand for round-the-clock carbon-free energy.
AES_2021q4: AES entered Q3 2021 after a strong August reaction, with an 8.5 GW backlog already built and very strong technology-customer demand signaled, raising the bar to continued acceleration, not just maintenance. The quarter also included the Fluence IPO process and ongoing coal retirements, sharpening focus on the clean-energy platforms' value.
AES_2022q2: AES entered Q1 2022 with a renewables backlog above 9 GW and strong momentum in large technology-customer contracts, but new macro risks emerged: supply-chain constraints, inflation and rising rates threatening project costs and schedules. Approaching full investment-grade status offered a counterweight, potentially lowering the financing penalty on its buildout.
AES_2022q4: The second half of 2022 was dominated by rising rates, inflation and supply-chain risk, all potential headwinds for a capital-intensive renewables developer, offset by AES's long-term contracted model, investment-grade credit and large PPA backlog. November guidance nudged fiscal-2022 EPS to about $1.65, signaling improving confidence despite the macro backdrop.
AES_2023q1: AES entered the 2022 year-end report with a large renewables backlog but a tough macro setup, as higher rates pressured utility and renewable-development stocks broadly. Investors wanted proof AES could keep growing adjusted EPS despite financing costs and supply-chain normalization, with 2023 guidance mattering more than the trailing quarter.
AES_2023q2: AES entered Q1 2023 with 2023 adjusted EPS guidance of $1.65-1.75 and a strategy concentrated in renewables, U.S. utilities and new energy technologies, plus a plan to fully exit coal by end-2025. The question was whether renewable construction could overcome higher interest expense, weaker LNG margins and utility weather swings.
AES_2023q3: By August 2023 AES had reframed itself around four strategic business units and a 6%-8% growth target through 2027, with focus on renewable project completion and utility rate-base growth. The 2023 EPS range of $1.65-1.75 was maintained heading into the report, so no guidance reset was expected.
AES_2023q4: AES entered Q3 after a large August selloff, leaving investors more sensitive to interest rates and project-delivery risk even as the renewables backlog and utility growth thesis stayed intact. The bar was lower after the decline, but investors needed proof 2023 earnings would land above the low end of $1.65-1.75.
AES_2024q2: AES entered Q1 2024 after a strong 2023 finish — full-year adjusted EPS hit $1.76, 5.6 GW of renewables contracts signed, and 3.5 GW of construction completed — plus a February guidance raise strengthening confidence in the platform. May's question was whether backlog conversion could continue while controlling financing risk.
AES_2024q3: Between May and August 2024, AES leaned into technology-customer demand, agreeing to sell its AES Brasil stake for roughly $640 million while expanding its renewables pipeline. The prior quarter produced a large EPS beat but only a modest reaction, so execution needed to show earnings moving toward guidance top end.
AES_2024q4: AES entered Q3 2024 with the stock supported by an improving EPS outlook and record data-center hyperscaler sales, plus a new CDPQ partnership backing AES Ohio's growth. The prior report had already raised the low end of 2024 EPS expectations to $1.92, so October's hurdle was materially higher.
AGCO_2017q1: AGCO entered February 2017 near the bottom of a multi-year agricultural-equipment downturn, with 2016 spent restructuring and cutting production. Investors focused less on absolute sales and more on whether weak farm income, low commodity prices and dealer destocking were finally stabilizing rather than deepening.
AGCO_2017q3: AGCO entered Q2 2017 with investors watching whether the trough identified in February was becoming a genuine recovery. Western Europe and South America were stabilizing while North America stayed constrained, so a raised sales outlook would carry more weight than a single-quarter beat by signaling a broader recovery.
AGCO_2017q4: AGCO entered Q3 2017 after a July guidance raise, shifting the narrative from trough-stabilization to earnings recovery. The bar was higher: strong volume needed to translate into margin progress rather than being absorbed by engineering investment and material costs, or the stock could react negatively despite a decent quarter.
AGCO_2018q1: AGCO entered Q4 2017 after a strong Q3 beat and favorable estimate revisions, so the market expected another beat rather than mere stabilization. The thesis rested on continued sales growth, margin expansion and constructive 2018 guidance as farm income recovered, raising the stakes on any disappointment.
AGCO_2018q2: AGCO entered Q1 2018 after a February EPS miss but an intact operating recovery, so investors wanted to know if that was a one-quarter blip. Trade-war fears had emerged, making farm-equipment stocks newly sensitive to China/U.S. headlines, so a guidance raise would be especially informative.
AGCO_2018q3: AGCO entered Q2 2018 after a strong Q1 report that initially drew a negative reaction but shares had since risen about 7% as investors warmed to guidance. South America remained weak against improving North America and Europe, so a beat needed to show strong regions could offset the laggard.
AGCO_2018q4: AGCO entered Q3 2018 with strong North American and European momentum but lingering doubt about the global farm-equipment recovery's durability. Q2 had beaten on both EPS and revenue while South America stayed weak, leaving investors focused on whether pricing could offset raw-material inflation and trade uncertainty.
AGCO_2019q1: AGCO entered Q4 2018 after a strong Q3 beat, but trade tensions and weaker crop economics had made the macro backdrop more cyclical again. Investors wanted proof pricing and productivity initiatives could sustain earnings and give the company enough operating leverage to offset softer 2019 demand.
AGCO_2019q2: AGCO entered Q1 2019 with the stock up 28.3% year to date at a new 52-week high on repeated earnings beats. February's report reinforced that with a large EPS beat and improving EME profitability, so May faced a high bar built on continued margin expansion outrunning revenue growth.
AGCO_2019q3: AGCO entered Q2 2019 after an extraordinary Q1 EPS beat of over 100% had made margin expansion the dominant narrative, even as agricultural demand stayed uneven amid trade tensions. Investors wanted proof the profit surge could persist even if top-line growth softened, setting an unusually high bar.
AGCO_2019q4: AGCO entered Q3 2019 after two straight quarters of margin and EPS beats despite soft revenue, with trade uncertainty and weak farm economics constraining demand. The market could tolerate some sales weakness if EPS kept beating, but watched for signs volume contraction was too large for cost actions to offset.
AGCO_2020q1: AGCO entered Q4 2019 after EPS held up despite weak sales and the stock outperformed for a month after. Zacks expected about $1.55 EPS, with shares already up 12.1% over the prior year versus a declining industry, testing whether pricing/productivity gains could keep compensating for a difficult farm cycle.
AGCO_2020q2: AGCO entered Q1 2020 after a weak February report, then the COVID-19 shock hit — guidance was withdrawn, China and Europe factories disrupted, and a $520 million term loan added for liquidity. Investors were assessing demand destruction, factory continuity and dealer support, not just cyclical margin offset.
AGCO_2020q3: AGCO entered Q2 2020 after Q1 showed more resilience than feared, but April-June carried the full impact of European and South American factory shutdowns. Agricultural demand was proving sturdier than other industrial markets, so earnings sensitivity centered on production availability and reopening pace rather than a demand collapse.
AGCO_2020q4: AGCO entered Q3 2020 with a recovery thesis: factories reopening, resilient farm demand, and a strong order board to work through after the shutdown-heavy second quarter. Investors wanted proof deferred production could convert into sales and margins without new supply-chain bottlenecks as farm economics improved into autumn.
AGCO_2022q1: AGCO entered Q4 2021 after an exceptionally strong cycle — Q2 2021 sales grew 43.5% with record EPS — but management flagged severe material inflation and supply-chain pressure. The question was no longer demand but whether AGCO could convert a strong order book into profitable shipments amid component shortages.
AGCO_2022q2: AGCO entered Q1 2022 after Q4 beat EPS by over 70% with above-consensus 2022 guidance, an already demanding setup. Russia's invasion of Ukraine added commodity, currency and input-cost volatility that was simultaneously supportive of some regions' farm income and disruptive to AGCO's supply chain, making regional mix critical.
AGCO_2022q3: AGCO entered Q2 2022 after two consecutive major EPS beats, with inflation, shortages and currency pressure still intense. Already-high full-year guidance needed Q2 to prove the earnings trajectory could survive a stronger dollar and ongoing supply friction, as the market began weighing whether commodity prices had peaked.
AGCO_2022q4: AGCO entered Q3 2022 with strong demand but a maturing cycle. Q2 beat EPS while missing revenue on currency, with full-year guidance near $11.70-$11.90 EPS. The order backdrop stayed healthy in high-horsepower Fendt and precision products, so the risk shifted from lack of demand to sustaining unusually strong margins.
AGCO_2023q1: AGCO entered Q4 2022 with record operating margins and strong order boards, but investors debated whether the agricultural cycle had peaked after Q3 revenue missed despite record margins. Shares had already gained about 18% over the prior year, raising the bar for a large beat to move the stock further.
AGCO_2024q1: AGCO entered Q4 2023 after a record year in which management repeatedly raised guidance, but the narrative was turning from expansion to normalization. Investors cared less about 2023's strength and more about how steep the 2024 downturn would be, especially in South America where demand was already softening.
AGCO_2024q2: AGCO entered Q1 2024 after February formally shifted the story to declining equipment demand, so investors focused on the pace of deterioration and whether precision ag could offset it. AGCO completed the PTx Trimble joint venture (85% stake) April 1, adding a higher-margin platform but complicating comparisons.
AGCO_2024q3: AGCO entered Q2 2024 with the farm-equipment downturn accelerating after Q1's lower sales and margins, so July's report tested the depth of production cuts and guidance reduction. AGCO began consolidating PTx Trimble and, on July 25, agreed to sell its Grain & Protein business, adding transition complexity.
AGCO_2024q4: AGCO entered Q3 2024 after a major July reset — Q2 missed EPS and revenue and cut full-year guidance from roughly $12 to $8 EPS as management deliberately cut production. Investors expected a very weak environment and questioned whether the reset was deep enough despite PTx Trimble's higher-margin promise.
AIR_2017q1: AAR entered March 2017 with healthy aftermarket activity and expanding supply-chain management, having recently won an A320 component-repair deal with Allegiant and landing-gear overhaul work for SkyWest. The question was whether these customer wins would translate into sustained revenue growth beyond fluctuating legacy government and expeditionary programs.
AIR_2017q4: AAR entered fiscal Q2 2018 with commercial aviation-services growing on supply-chain and parts programs, plus a ramping State Department WASS contract requiring execution. The riskier Expeditionary portfolio faced ending contracts and asset exposure, so investors had to separate the quality of the growing core business from legacy non-core risk.
AIR_2018q1: AAR entered March 2018 after a December impairment had dented confidence in the Expeditionary portfolio, though core Aviation Services stayed healthy. New WASS and Air Force landing-gear awards offered a revenue bridge to offset the KC-10 CLS wind-down, needed as proof the prior loss was a cleanup, not a trend.
AIR_2018q4: AAR entered fiscal Q2 2019 with double-digit Aviation Services growth and new awards centering the thesis on parts supply, distribution and programs over legacy expeditionary assets. Airframe MRO activity was softer, so investors needed evidence growth in higher-demand businesses could outweigh that weakness while scaling execution stayed clean.
AIR_2019q1: AAR entered fiscal Q3 2019 with strong momentum — 17% sales growth and 51% adjusted-EPS growth in December — but a European airline bankruptcy created a new charge and visible credit risk. Parts supply, programs and WASS were still expanding, so investors watched for continued growth without another surprise.
AIR_2019q4: AAR entered fiscal Q2 2020 with fiscal 2019 sales up 17.4% to about $2.05 billion and adjusted EPS up 36%, driven by parts supply and programs. The market had moved past questioning growth itself to whether it could persist at scale and support a higher full-year guidance path.
AIR_2020q1: AAR entered March 2020 with strong momentum after guidance was raised on 14% revenue growth, right as COVID-19 collapsed passenger traffic and forced groundings. Investors shifted from tracking guidance to estimating how much business would vanish, how fast costs could be cut, and whether defense exposure offered stability.
AIR_2020q4: AAR entered fiscal Q2 2021 after a year resizing for the commercial-aviation collapse — Q4 2020 sales fell 26% and management restructured and exited underperforming lines. By December the question had shifted from survival to the pace of recovery and durability of cost cuts, with government exposure providing stability.
AIR_2021q1: AAR entered fiscal Q3 2021 with investors already pricing a recovery, after aggressive 2020 cost cuts and improving vaccine-driven travel expectations. The key question was whether revenue would turn before temporary CARES Act support faded, requiring investors to separate that one-time aid from the business's underlying adjusted earnings power.
AIR_2021q4: AAR entered fiscal Q2 2022 in a much-improved demand environment, with commercial flight activity recovering and government exposure plus a leaner cost structure intact. Investors wanted evidence reopening would drive both revenue growth and sustained EPS recovery, with capital allocation gaining importance as balance-sheet risk receded post-restructuring.
AIR_2022q1: AAR entered fiscal Q3 2022 after adjusted EPS rose 71% in December and a $150 million buyback was authorized, tying the recovery thesis to rising aircraft utilization converting into parts, MRO and program revenue. Fuel-price spikes and Russia's invasion of Ukraine added a new risk just as passenger demand recovered.
AIR_2022q4: AAR entered fiscal Q2 2023 with the commercial recovery well established after strong EPS and sales growth from normalizing flight activity. Focus was shifting from reopening growth toward margin expansion, labor availability and demand sustainability, since easy comparisons to pandemic-depressed quarters were fading and the base was now more normal.
AIR_2023q1: AAR entered fiscal Q3 2023 with 8% sales growth and 30% adjusted-EPS growth in December confirming a mature recovery, then answered the next strategic question one day before earnings by acquiring Trax, an aircraft MRO/fleet-management software provider expected to add higher-margin recurring revenue and be adjusted-EPS accretive.
AIR_2023q4: AAR entered fiscal Q2 2024 with shares already up roughly 33% year to date and 71% over twelve months after a strong Q1 ($0.78 EPS, $549.7 million revenue), leaving elevated expectations. Having reshaped its portfolio via Trax, investors also watched the pricing and margin profile of any further acquisition strategy.
AIR_2024q1: AAR entered fiscal Q3 2024 having closed the $725 million Triumph Product Support deal March 1, funded via a $550 million notes offering and expanded revolver. The deal added specialized MRO capability and Asia-Pacific reach, but transaction costs and higher leverage made adjusted results more informative than GAAP profit.
